reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .303, 100th percentile, and that's the cleanest way to understand what he is: a shortstop who makes hard contact so consistently that the batting average question is essentially settled before the season starts. His 52.2% hard-hit rate pairs with a 92.7 mph average exit velocity, both sitting in the 94th-95th percentile range, and the .382 xwOBA says the production is fully load-bearing. The one real tension in the profile is a 33.3% chase rate that grades out in the bottom third of the league, which is why the projection at .285/.354/.460 comes in somewhat below what the raw contact quality might suggest if the plate discipline ever sharpened. Add 30.2 ft/s sprint speed at the 99th percentile and 42 projected steals and you have a profile that doesn't need the walk rate to improve — he's already one of the most complete position players in this class.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting card reads like two separate elite hitters stacked on top of each other: a .405 xwOBA and 16.4% barrel rate that belong to a pure masher, sitting alongside a 13.7% walk rate that belongs to a disciplined table-setter. The catch is a 30.4% whiff rate that keeps the strikeout number honest at 23.0% K, which is why the projection lands at .286/.390/.545 rather than something gaudy — he gives back some contact, and that's just the shape of this bat. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA with a 30.4% whiff rate against hitters and only a 3.8% barrel rate allowed is a genuine frontline arm, full stop. The whole profile hinges on staying healthy enough to do both, and if the pitching workload gets curtailed again, you still have one of baseball's most dangerous offensive players buried in the Dodgers lineup.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile here is as loud as it gets: a 20.8% barrel rate and a 95.1 mph average exit velocity both sitting at the 100th percentile, with an xSLG of .585 that says the projection's .523 SLG is conservative. Wood also runs a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitter at this level can match. The whole thing hinges on whether a 28.6% strikeout rate, bottom 12% of the league, ever comes down, because at the current whiff rate the gap between what he should hit and what he actually hits stays wide. reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact-and-strike zone piece is the only thing keeping a .365 xwOBA from being a clean superstar profile. De La Cruz's 93.8 mph average exit velocity sits in the 98th percentile, his 14.1% barrel rate is genuinely elite, and 51.1% hard-hit keeps the production from being a small cluster of lucky ABs. The hang is the 26.6% strikeout rate, which drags his actual outcomes well below what the contact quality deserves. If the zone management he's shown, 10.8% walk rate against a 26.0% chase rate, holds and the K% trends even modestly downward, the projection's .268/.349/.489 undersells him; if the whiff rate at 27.9% stays where it is, you're living with a boom-or-bust lineup piece who puts up 28 home runs and 31 stolen bases but leaves too many at-bats on the floor.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The barrel rate tells the story here: 13.9% puts Stewart in the 89th percentile, and the .466 xSLG confirms the raw power is translating into genuine hard contact. The gap between that xSLG and the pedestrian 39.4% Hard-Hit rate is the interesting wrinkle, because he's barreling balls at an elite clip without generating elite hard-hit volume, meaning he's feasting on a narrower band of contact quality than a typical 33-homer hitter. His 10.2% walk rate is quiet and real, and the projection's .801 OPS across 691 PA reads as a floor if the barrel rate holds at its current shape. Everything hinges on whether the 22.1% strikeout rate creeps up as pitchers attack the 26.7% whiff rate more aggressively; if the contact quality stays this tilted toward barrels, he's a legitimate middle-of-the-order piece in Cincinnati for a long time.

Walker's 92.6 mph average exit velocity sits at the 94th percentile, his barrel rate is 13.3%, and those two things together tell you the raw damage is genuine when he makes contact. The problem is a 35.3% chase rate and a 31.0% whiff rate that together leave him exposed to pitchers who can locate off the plate, which is why the projection has him at a .277/.335/.475 line rather than something that matches his xSLG of .485. reports.name: Miguel Vargas
reports.published_report: The gap between his .381 xwOBA and his actual production is the whole argument for Vargas. His 14.2% barrel rate and a 22.3% chase rate that ranks in the top ten percent of the league say the contact quality and the plate discipline are both genuinely elite-tier, yet the batting average hasn't followed because the xBA sits at .261, solid but not special, which means he's hitting the ball hard into outs more than he's getting robbed. The projection resolves most of that gap: 32 home runs, a .340 OBP, and 15 stolen bags across 697 plate appearances is a legitimate middle-of-the-order profile, and it holds as long as the barrel rate and chase discipline stay where the current Statcast numbers show them. The one honest drag is the fielding, which grades out near the bottom of the position, so if the power translates and the 12.9% walk rate holds, he's a clear everyday regular, and if the contact fortune keeps running against him while the glove limits his positional flexibility, he's a useful but expensive DH type.

reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: The xBA-to-xSLG split tells you exactly what Stott is: a contact-first second baseman whose bat-to-ball ability grades well above average while the raw power sits squarely in the middle of the pack. His 19.0% whiff rate is the quietest reason he's useful, letting a 9.8% walk rate play up and keeping an .OBP projection of .338 honest across a full 586 projected plate appearances. The 29 projected steals are where the profile gets interesting, because a 28.4 ft/s sprint speed in the 79th percentile is a real asset attached to a lineup spot where he'll get chances to use it. If the contact quality holds, he's a solid everyday second baseman whose value accumulates through rate and run-scoring contribution rather than power peaks; if the contact-over-power profile starts slipping with age, what's left is a useful platoon and baserunning piece.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The exit velocity picture is exceptional, 85.7 mph average exit velo at the 97th percentile, and the contact quality backs it up with a 3.65 xERA that looks like a mid-rotation contributor in a good lineup. The problem is obvious in the walk rate: 13.0% is an 8th-percentile number, and when Brown can't control the zone, his 26.3% chase rate (also bottom-of-the-barrel) means hitters can simply wait him out rather than expand. He generates whiffs at a fine clip and keeps barrels down as well as anyone, so the stuff is clearly there to miss bats and suppress damage when he's near the zone. The whole profile hinges on whether he can find even mediocre command, and if the walk rate doesn't come down, the 110.4 projected innings and 3.67 ERA are probably the ceiling rather than the floor.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .837 projected OPS is doing real work here, and the Statcast profile tells you why it's plausible: an 11.0% barrel rate against a .223 xBA is the clearest possible signal of a guy who hits the ball hard in the air but can't hit it often enough to sustain a real average. The .298 xwOBA sits in the bottom fifth of the league, and a 41.2% chase rate with a 5.6% walk rate means pitchers have an easy blueprint. Coors Field is carrying the .267/.309 projection line more than the underlying contact quality warrants. If the chase rate tightens even a little he's a 25-homer bat with a playable OBP; if it doesn't, he's a streaky power corner outfielder who needs the altitude to look like a starter.

reports.name: Jacob Wilson
reports.published_report: The contact grades out elite, the power doesn't. Wilson's 11.4% strikeout rate sits in the 96th percentile, and his xBA of .265 tracks accordingly, but an 84.1 mph average exit velocity and 2.5% barrel rate explain why the xSLG lands at .348 and the projection carries just 11 projected home runs across 512 plate appearances. He puts the ball in play constantly and almost never whiffs, which is genuinely valuable, but a 3.6% walk rate means he isn't working counts deep enough to compensate for the soft contact when pitchers locate. The whole profile hinges on the 97th-percentile fielding — if that OAA holds at shortstop, there's a real everyday player here despite the bat-side limitations; if the glove regresses, you're left with a light-hitting infielder who hits for average and not much else.

reports.name: Lawrence Butler
reports.published_report: The Statcast card is a contradiction in cleats: a 79th-percentile chase rate sitting right next to a 25th-percentile xBA and a 20th-percentile xSLG. Butler lays off breaking stuff in the dirt as well as most hitters in the league, but when he connects, the ball doesn't go anywhere damaging, and a 27.3% whiff rate keeps punching holes in the contact side of the ledger. The 11.4% walk rate is the one skill that translates cleanly, keeping his .303 projected OBP alive even as the .215 average does its damage. If the contact quality ever catches up to the discipline, there's a second-division regular hiding in here; if it doesn't, 14 projected steals and a walk rate don't add up to a full-time job.

reports.name: Nolan Schanuel
reports.published_report: The gap between a 13.4% strikeout rate and a 2.5% barrel rate is the whole profile: Schanuel makes an unusual amount of contact, and almost none of it does damage. His xBA sits at .280 with contact quality that ranks in the bottom quarter of the league by exit velocity, which means the batting average holds up while the power ceiling stays as a genuine constraint, not a developmental gap waiting to close. The projection, .272/.351/.392 with 11 home runs, is probably close to the floor and the ceiling at once for a 24-year-old first baseman whose value lives entirely in on-base skills and a strong glove. If the barrel rate creeps up even modestly, the OBP profile supports a solid regular; if it stays at 2.5%, he's a useful piece in the right lineup construction but thin for the position.

reports.name: Dylan Cease
reports.published_report: A 36.1% strikeout rate at the 99th percentile is the whole engine, and the 34.9% whiff rate confirms hitters are genuinely lost against his stuff. The one number that complicates the portrait is a 10.6% walk rate sitting at the 24th percentile, which means the strikeout volume is always partly funding free passes. The contact-suppression underneath is legitimate: a 4.7% barrel rate, an average exit velocity of 86.0 mph, and an xERA of 2.74 all point to a pitcher whose stuff dismantles barrels rather than one who benefits from weak sequencing. The projection at 2.63 ERA over 179.9 innings with 253 strikeouts is believable if the walk rate stays manageable, and it unravels only if the command drifts further and the free passes start compounding against his pitch count.

reports.name: Luke Adams
reports.published_report: The discipline-power combination at AAA is legitimate: 33 walks against only 37 strikeouts in 261 plate appearances, with a .252 ISO that translates to .18 at the MLB level. That's a hitter making contact, taking pitches, and doing real damage when he connects. The BABIP sitting at .245 means the .252 average is running below what the underlying profile suggests, so the .401 OBP is carrying itself almost entirely on plate discipline rather than fortunate contact. The translation puts his walk rate above league average and his strikeout rate well below it, which at first base means everything hinges on whether the power holds against better velocity — if it does, he's a low-end everyday regular; if it doesn't, you're left with a patient, light-hitting first baseman who is a bench bat at best.

reports.name: Munetaka Murakami
reports.published_report: The contact-to-power disconnect here is about as wide as it gets: a 94.2 mph average exit velocity and 20.8% barrel rate that both grade at the top of the sport, paired with a 42.5% whiff rate that sits near the bottom. He doesn't chase, walking at 17.1%, which tells you this is a swing-and-miss problem on pitches he offers at, not a recognition problem. The projection (.233/.361/.514) reflects exactly what that looks like in a full season: massive power output, a batting average that bleeds, and an OBP that climbs back up because pitchers can't afford to attack him. Thirty-seven projected home runs is the floor if the barrel rate holds; the ceiling question is whether he ever tightens contact enough to stop surrendering the gap between his .233 average and .361 OBP.

reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .232 and the xERA is 2.22, both sitting at the 99th percentile, and the chase rate of 37.1% explains most of it. Hitters are expanding the zone against him at a rate that puts him in the 96th percentile, and when they do make contact, a 4.1% barrel rate keeps the damage contained even when the hard-hit numbers aren't historically suppressed. reports.name: Jake McCarthy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a puzzle with one very loud piece. His 85.1 mph average exit velocity and 27.0% hard-hit rate sit at the bottom of the league, yet his xBA grades out well above average, because he's hitting the ball where it goes and moving at 29.9 ft/s — a sprint speed that lives in a tier almost nobody else occupies. The projection's .295/.337/.488 line in 555 PA leans heavily on that speed translating into hits on contact that a slower player simply doesn't reach, and his 4.7% walk rate is thin enough that if the batted-ball luck normalizes downward, there's no patience backstop to catch the fall. What he is, if it holds, is a legitimately useful everyday outfielder at a Coors address; what's left without the sprint-driven BABIP is a bench bat who chases too much and doesn't hit it hard enough to compensate.

reports.name: Masyn Winn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a study in mismatched halves. His chase rate sits at 24.4%, which is a genuine plus tool, the kind of zone discipline that usually anchors a real offensive profile, but the power side undercuts everything: a 3.2% barrel rate and .335 xSLG that both sit near the bottom of the league. The contact quality just isn't there to make the plate discipline matter the way it should. What holds this whole thing together at shortstop is the 98th-percentile OAA and 28.4 ft/s sprint speed, because if his bat settles around that .305 xwOBA, the value equation runs almost entirely through his glove and legs. The projection (.247/.320/.342 across 624 PA) looks about right: an everyday shortstop whose floor is defensible and whose ceiling depends entirely on whether the exit velocity climbs enough to let the discipline breathe.

reports.name: Bryce Miller
reports.published_report: A 2.74 xERA with a 4.9% walk rate tells you most of what you need to know: Miller suppresses contact as well as almost anyone, and he almost never beats himself. The 36.2% chase rate is the engine, pulling hitters out of the zone rather than depending on swing-and-miss within it, which explains why his whiff rate sits in the middle of the pack while his hard-hit rate and xwOBA both land in the top tier. The projection at 3.45 ERA over 125.3 innings is the honest reckoning: a pitcher who misses bats at a league-average clip will be more ERA than xERA when sequencing normalizes, and 125.3 innings flags the health question as the real variable. If he stays in a rotation and holds the chase rate, he's a solid mid-rotation arm with legitimate ace-adjacent underlying numbers; if the innings don't materialize, those elite contact-suppression marks are just a highlight reel on a limited workload.

reports.name: Angel Genao
reports.published_report: The contact-and-patience combo is what makes this profile hum. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Genao is hitting .300/.401/.474 through 419 plate appearances, with 60 walks against just 68 strikeouts — a discipline profile that translates to an 11.5 BB% and a K% sitting below league average at the MLB level. The power is the open question: his .174 ISO in the minors translates to .141 at the MLB equivalent, a tick below average, which means if he doesn't add loft or pull-side juice, he becomes a shortstop who gets on base rather than one who damages you. If the hit tool holds and the walks travel, he grows into a low-end everyday regular; if the power translation stays thin, what's left is a bench bat who can still take a walk.

reports.name: Kyle Stowers
reports.published_report: The contact is the problem, and the problem is severe. Stowers hits the ball as hard as almost anyone, with a 55.0% hard-hit rate and 92.1 mph average exit velocity, but a 35.4% whiff rate means he doesn't make enough contact for that raw power to show up in the batting average column, which is why his xBA sits at .235 even as his xSLG reaches .436. The projection threads that needle into a .779 OPS with 23 home runs across a full season, which is a useful offensive profile if you squint past the .240 average, but the whole thing collapses if his strikeout rate, already at 31.3%, creeps any higher. He's either a power-first regular with a tolerable strikeout tax or a platoon piece whose at-bats against good velocity pitchers become unplayable, and right now the Statcast profile doesn't tell you which.

reports.name: Dillon Dingler

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the one tension point in an otherwise clean profile. At 19.0%, Alcantara sits well below the league median for a frontline starter, yet the contact he allows is managed so well that it barely matters: barrels against him at 5.7% and a walk rate of 6.2% that grades near the top of the league tell you he controls both the plate and the damage. A 97.5 mph fastball gives him the ceiling to beat hitters through velocity alone when the chase rate dips, and the .296 xwOBA confirms that the underlying quality of contact is genuinely suppressed, not a product of sequencing luck. The profile hinges on durability, and 214.7 projected innings is an argument in itself, because if he stays upright he profiles as a true number-two starter, the kind who accumulates quality starts in bunches without needing a swing-and-miss carrying the load.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci

He's a speed-and-contact profile that works until pitchers decide the soft contact is a feature, not a bug, and start attacking him in the zone without consequence. Low-end everyday outfielder is the ceiling if the discipline holds; a useful but limited bench piece if it doesn't.

reports.name: Kyle Harrison
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile reads cleaner than the surface results have suggested: a 3.27 xERA, a 29.7% strikeout rate, and a 6.3% walk rate is a genuine two-way weapons profile. Harrison gets whiffs and he limits free passes, which is the combination that makes a strikeout rate mean something. The exit velocity numbers are middling, but they're downstream of the strikeout and contact-suppression work, and a 29.0% whiff rate explains why contact quality ends up manageable anyway. ValuCast projects a 3.60 ERA over 132.4 innings, a modest step back from what the xERA implies, and that gap is the honest tension here: the profile holds if he faces enough traffic to strand, collapses if the strand rate regresses and the fastball at 94.9 mph doesn't generate enough weak contact to bail him out. The ceiling is a mid-rotation workhorse; if the zone command slips, he's a useful arm eating innings at the back.

If the speed and glove hold up as everyday contributors he's a fringe regular worth a roster spot; if the contact quality stays at the basement, he's a defensive specialist asking to hit too high in the order.

reports.name: Sean Burke

If the ride on the fastball flattens, he becomes a back-end innings-eater rather than the mid-rotation workhorse this projection describes.

reports.name: Austin Riley

reports.name: Jake Burger
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are ugly, but the power contact is legitimate. Burger's 46.2% hard-hit rate and 10.8% barrel rate describe a hitter who punishes mistakes even when he misses a lot, and the projection's 27 home runs over a full 628 PA season follows logically from that shape. The problem is the 34.6% whiff rate and 36.9% chase rate, which together explain why an xSLG of .388 collapses into a .296 xwOBA, because he's not getting to that power often enough against quality stuff. He profiles as a useful RBI corner bat in a lineup that can absorb the .236/.296 on-base drag, and if pitchers ever stop burying breaking balls out of the zone, the ceiling ticks up, but the whiff-and-chase combination is too chronic to bet against.

report_llm.text: The ISO is .296 across AA & A+, and at 20 years old that's not a number you see very often. The problem is the strikeouts: 128 punchouts in 463 plate appearances, translating to 30% at the major-league level, well above what most big-league hitters run, and the contact floor is thin enough that the whole power story depends on whether he can tighten his zone coverage as pitchers get sharper. Walk rate translates to 11% at the majors, better than the big-league norm, so the eye is genuinely there, but the K-BB gap leaves the average (.246 across AA & A+) propped up by a .286 BABIP with room to fall. If the strikeouts don't come down, what's left is a bench bat with loud raw power and not enough contact to start; if he makes even modest adjustments, the ISO-plus-walk combination becomes a regular's profile at third.

reports.name: Kevin Alcántara
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loud number: .273 at AAA across 284 plate appearances, translating to .191 at the MLB level against a pool where .15 is ordinary. The strikeout concern carries over just as cleanly — 30% at AAA becomes 28% translated, and that gap between his power and his contact shapes everything about what he becomes. Walk rate translates to 10.4%, which keeps the OBP from collapsing and tells you the plate discipline isn't nothing, but pitchers will test the swing and the results will determine the ceiling. If the contact doesn't tighten, he's a bench bat who can punish a mistake; if it does, there's a second-division regular in here somewhere.

Hardin has posted a 2.9 BB/9 across those same 101 innings, and when you translate the control profile to an MLB equivalent it comes out to 3.2 BB/9, right where MLB average sits, with K-BB% landing at 13.9% against the 13.5% MLB average. The strikeouts are present, 115 of them across AAA & AA, but the ERA says the stuff isn't suppressing contact well enough to see more than a depth arm here, and the ceiling and floor are essentially the same answer. reports.name: Brody Hopkins
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 106 punchouts across 85 AAA innings translate to a 9.4 K/9 in MLB context, respectable company, but the walk rate buries everything underneath it. At AAA he's posting 9.2 BB/9, and translated to the big-league level that comes out to 7.3, more than double what a typical MLB starter allows; the K-BB% sits at just 5 percent at AAA, and the MLB equivalent lands at 7.4 where the league norm is 13.5. Eighty-seven walks in 85 innings is a pitcher who is actively battling himself more than hitters. If the control ever firms up, the strikeout rate is a real foundation to build on, but right now the only realistic outcome is a depth arm, and that ceiling only gets reached if the walk rate falls enough to make the strikeouts matter.

reports.name: J.T. Ginn
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is genuinely good — 5.6% barrel rate, 34.7% hard-hit rate, 87.1 mph average exit velocity, all sitting in the upper quarter of the league, and then you scroll to the walk rate. At 10.4% BB%, Ginn is near the bottom of qualified starters, and a strikeout rate of 21.1% doesn't give him enough margin to survive those free passes. The whiff numbers at 27.4% say the stuff plays in the zone; the problem is he's not forcing enough hitters out of it, with a 30.0% chase rate that's right at the middle of the pack. If the walk rate compresses even modestly, the 3.66 ERA projection starts to look credible against a 4.00 xERA; if it doesn't, he's a back-end arm eating innings for a bad Athletics rotation while the gap between his contact suppression and his command keeps the ceiling low.

reports.name: Nathan Flewelling
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the most interesting thing here, and it almost obscures everything else. At A+ this year, Flewelling has drawn 67 walks in 434 plate appearances, a 15% clip that translates to an 11.3% MLB-equivalent rate, and his 83rd-percentile walk mark among peers is the clearest carrying tool in the profile. The power reads similarly loud at face value, 19 home runs and a .211 ISO, but the MLB-equivalent ISO lands at .146 against a .150 MLB average, which is the honest shape of things: a 19-year-old catcher whose discipline grades well and whose raw power may not fully survive the jump. The strikeout rate is where it gets complicated, 26% at A+ becoming a translated 29.6%, and a .239 average backed by a .293 BABIP doesn't leave much cushion if the K% doesn't tighten as he climbs. If the plate discipline holds and he sticks behind the dish, there's a low-end regular in here; if the strikeouts follow him up the ladder, what's left is a bench catcher who walks a lot but doesn't hit enough.

At A+ this year, Luke Stevenson has drawn 81 walks against 107 strikeouts across 379 plate appearances, a 21% walk rate that sits at the 98th percentile among hitters in the pool, and the power is credible enough, 16 home runs, a .245 ISO, an .OBP of .414, that he isn't simply taking pitches because he can't hit them. The translation is where the tension lives: that walk rate shrinks to 14.4% against big-league arms, the strikeout rate climbs to 30.7%, and the ISO lands at .161, just a tick above a league average that doesn't require much. The whole profile hinges on whether a catcher can carry a 30.7% strikeout rate in the majors and still generate enough contact quality to matter, and if he can't shorten up as pitching improves, this is a bench catcher with a good eye rather than a regular.

reports.name: Spencer Miles
reports.published_report: The contact suppression numbers are the story here. Miles sits at a 3.7% barrel rate and an average exit velocity of 86.4 mph against him, which tells you hitters are making contact but rarely doing anything with it — the xERA of 3.06 and xwOBA of .272 are downstream of that, not a mirage. What he doesn't have is swing-and-miss: an 18.4% whiff rate and 28.4% chase rate are both well below league average, meaning his 23.4% strikeout rate is about as high as this profile can generate, and it could easily slip. If his ability to limit hard contact holds, he's a useful middle-innings arm who eats innings at a 3.28 ERA with solid control at 6.5% walks; if hitters start squaring him up, the strikeouts aren't there to cover it, and this becomes a league-average depth piece fast.

reports.name: Brandon Nimmo
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile here is genuinely loud: a .373 xwOBA, .293 xBA, and 52.0% hard-hit rate all cluster near the top of the league, which means the projection's .272 average and .784 OPS are actually conservative relative to what the batted-ball shape keeps promising. The disconnect is the walk rate. At 8.1%, well below what you'd expect from a hitter who makes this kind of contact, he's leaving runs on the table that his earlier Mets incarnation used to collect, and if that gap doesn't close, the .342 OBP stays a ceiling rather than a floor. Still, 19 projected home runs across 656 plate appearances, backed by a .503 xSLG, says the power is translating regardless of the plate discipline slide. Everyday outfielder, no qualifier needed.

reports.name: Ernie Clement
reports.published_report: The gap between a 9.9% strikeout rate and a 3.2% walk rate is the whole profile in miniature: elite contact, almost no power, and zero patience to compensate. His xwOBA sits at .266 with a Hard-Hit% of 20.9%, both scraping the bottom of the league, which means the .279 projected AVG is doing almost all the offensive work. If his BABIP catches a cold, there's no walk rate to catch him and no over-the-fence power to offset the damage. The projection's 630 PA suggest someone will hand him a starting job, but what he is, honestly, is a bench infielder who can make enough contact to keep his average presentable as long as the balls keep finding holes.

reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the source of the problem. reports.name: Francisco Lindor
reports.published_report: The bat plays up more than the counting stats suggest. Lindor's 91.5 mph average exit velocity and 49.5% hard-hit rate sit well above the middle of the league, and his .354 xwOBA signals that the underlying contact quality has been genuine, not a product of soft-contact luck running hot. The projection's .247 AVG is the honest translation of a 70th-percentile xBA, a hitter who squares the ball hard but doesn't spray it everywhere, and the .441 SLG in 459 projected PA reflects a real gap between his raw power and how often he barrels things up, since that 9.8% barrel rate sits closer to average than his exit-velo profile implies. Everything here hinges on whether sprint speed at 26.6 ft/s, a 29th-percentile mark, continues to erode his range at short, because if the Mets have to move him off the position the defensive value that underwrites his everyday case leaves with him.

reports.name: Willy Adames
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .217 with a 27.7% strikeout rate tells the real story here: Adames makes enough contact to barrel it occasionally, but the contact quality consistently grades below average in a way that suppresses his average and on-base value. His 8.4% barrel rate is roughly league average, yet the 87.2 mph average exit velocity and 38.3% hard-hit rate both land in the bottom third of the league, meaning the barrels aren't supported by a broader foundation of quality contact. The projection's .224 average and .290 OBP reflect exactly that — a hitter whose 25 projected home runs come from volume at-bats and a swing calibrated for lift rather than consistent damage, and if the strikeout rate climbs further, the counting stats evaporate faster than the OPS suggests. He's a low-end everyday shortstop whose value is almost entirely tied to staying healthy enough to accumulate the 658 projected plate appearances.

reports.name: Josh Stephan
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here, and everything else is keeping up just enough. At AAA in 2026, 31 walks across 108 innings translates to a 92nd-percentile BB/9 among pitchers with meaningful samples, and the MLB equivalent puts that at 2.9 per nine, a tick better than the league mean. The trouble is the strikeouts: 102 punchouts in those same 108 innings look fine in isolation, but they translate to 7.8 per nine against a major-league context of 8.6, and the 5.20 ERA at AAA suggests the stuff isn't missing bats often enough to hold up when contact finds grass. If the control holds and the strikeout rate inches toward league average, you've got a back-end starter or long-man who earns a rotation spot in a thin year; if it doesn't, the floor is exactly what the ceiling says, a depth arm who commands the zone without the swing-and-miss to survive.

Left-handed depth arms can find roster spots on shape alone, but if the walk rate doesn't come down, that's the ceiling too.

reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Nate Snead
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. Across AA & A+, Snead has issued just 22 walks in 89 innings, a 2.2 BB/9 that ranks in the 95th percentile of the pitcher pool, and the MLB-equivalent translation comes out at 2.8 while the league sits at 3.2. The strikeout side is the problem: 76 punchouts across AA & A+ gives him a 7.7 K/9, and the MLB translation comes out at 6.9 where the league averages 8.6, which is why the K-BB% lands at 15% in the minor-league pool but shrinks to 11.3% once the run environment shifts. If the command holds at the upper levels and the stuff generates enough weak contact to compensate for below-average swing-and-miss, there's a back-end piece here; if it doesn't, the profile is a depth arm with a polished walk rate and not much else to carry it.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.
